title: Coalescer skimming and fairness guardrails playbook
summary: Working notes and playbook for an experiment series that introduces a lightweight 'skimming' path within the coalescer to reduce tail latency regressions caused by strict max-window batching while preserving throughput and fairness across classes of traffic.
body:
Purpose and motivation:

We observe recurring tail-latency spikes for small/interactive requests when coalescer settings aggressively optimize for throughput (large max_batch_ms, high batch_size targets). The standard age-weighted batching improves fairness but still leaves scenarios where a long-running head-of-line request blocks small subsequent requests until the full batch timeout expires. The skimming idea: allow the coalescer to opportunistically form a small fast-path batch by 'skimming' a few oldest pending requests when certain conditions are met (low queue depth for the target priority, high age dispersion), instead of waiting the full window or forcing a large batch. The goal is to reduce p99/p999 for latency-sensitive classes with minimal throughput regression for bulk classes.

Hypotheses:
- H1: Allowing small skims (batch size 2-8) when age gap > skim_age_threshold reduces p99 by 20-40ms on interactive workloads with mixed sizes.
- H2: A skim guardrail that triggers only when queue occupancy for batchable workers < occupancy_threshold keeps throughput within 2-3% of baseline.
- H3: Age-decay weighting combined with skim limits prevents starvation of bulk traffic; fairness metrics (share of served tokens per class) remain within 5% of baseline.

Experiment variables and knobs:
- skim_enabled: boolean (on/off)
- skim_min_size: int (2)
- skim_max_size: int (8)
- skim_age_threshold_ms: int (10, 25, 50)
- skim_queue_occupancy_threshold: float (0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
- max_coalescer_window_ms: int (20, 50, 100)
- age_decay_half_life_ms: int (50, 200)
- min_batch_fraction: float (0.1, 0.25) -- fraction of target batch size below which skimming is allowed
- class_weight_caps: string (per-priority caps to prevent continuous skimming of low-priority classes)

Testbed setup:
- Cluster: 4-GPU serving pool (A100-like), single instance per container, same model (redwood-7b-v1) quantized path.
- Workloads: mixed synthetic load generator with three classes:
  * interactive_short: 8-token prompts, high QPS bursts, latency-sensitive
  * interactive_long: 256-token prompts, low QPS
  * bulk_async: 1024-token prompts, throughput-oriented (background)
- Traffic pattern: 90s windows with bursty arrivals for interactive_short (Poisson bursts), steady background load for bulk_async.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99/p999 latency, mean throughput (tokens/sec), tokens per second per class, batch size distribution, queue occupancy histograms, fairness metric (served_tokens[class]/total_tokens), starvation incidents (>=3x baseline delay for queued requests).

Baseline config used for comparison:
- max_coalescer_window_ms: 100
- target_batch_tokens: 4096
- age_weighting: enabled (half_life_ms=200)
- dynamic_timeouts: enabled
- no skimming (skim_enabled=false)

Example skim config (JSON blob as string for reference):
{
  "skim_enabled": true,
  "skim_min_size": 2,
  "skim_max_size": 6,
  "skim_age_threshold_ms": 25,
  "skim_queue_occupancy_threshold": 0.5,
  "min_batch_fraction": 0.15
}

Run plan (short):
1) Smoke run with skim_enabled=true, skim_age_threshold_ms=25, skim_max_size=6, baseline window=100ms. 10 repeats.
2) Sweep skim_age_threshold_ms in {10,25,50} holding skim_max_size=4, occupancy=0.5. 20 repeats each.
3) Sweep occupancy_threshold in {0.2,0.5,0.8} holding age_threshold=25ms.
4) Combined sweep with max_coalescer_window_ms in {20,50,100} to measure collateral throughput loss.
5) Long-run stability test: 6 hours with production-mixed trace and skim_enabled=true, capture outliers.

Observed results (notes from first 3 runs):
- Smoke run (10 reps): median p99 reduction for interactive_short = ~35ms (std 8ms). Throughput drop for bulk_async ~1.8% (within expected). Batch size distribution: small bump in 2-6 token batches across interactive classes.
- Age threshold sweep: 10ms reduced p50 marginally but increased number of tiny skims that slightly hurt throughput; 50ms reduced skim frequency, p99 benefit diminished. Sweet spot around 20-30ms.
- Occupancy sweep: occupancy_threshold=0.2 was too conservative (not enough skims -> no p99 benefit). occupancy_threshold=0.8 allowed skims that occasionally starved bulk windows leading to 4-6% throughput loss. 0.5 is the best tradeoff in our testbed.

Quantitative snapshot (representative):
- Baseline (no skim): interactive_short p99 = 210ms, p95=85ms, throughput_total = 480k tokens/s
- Skim config (age=25ms, max_size=6, occupancy=0.5): interactive_short p99 = 175ms, p95=78ms, throughput_total = 472k tokens/s
- Bulk_async token throughput delta: -1.8%
- Fairness (served_tokens fraction for interactive_short): +3.2% vs baseline (acceptable)

Failure modes and caveats:
- Excessive skimming on background-heavy nodes can fragment batches and increase per-token overhead; need global node-level occupancy gating.
- If model setup has heavy cold-KV-cache cost per request (rare for LLMs due to KV reuse), skims may increase wall time because of increased context switching between small and large batches.
- SKIM + dynamic_quantization heuristic interactions need auditing; if quantized fast path has different throughput char, small skims can change kernel selection frequency.

Operational rollout recommendations:
- Feature flag behind runtime flag and per-pool gate. Start with pool-level skim_enabled=false; enable per-customer pools with manual opt-in for latency-sensitive customers.
- Default guardrail: skim_age_threshold_ms=25, skim_max_size=6, occupancy_threshold=0.5, min_batch_fraction=0.12.
- Add per-route telemetry: skim_count, skim_success (skims that got scheduled within target latency), skim_abort_reasons (occupancy, class_cap, other).
- Add regression tests to CI that run microbench with synthetic interactive_short workload and assert p99 reduction or no more than 3% throughput regression in bulk mode.

Follow-ups / open questions:
- Do we want to expose skim knobs in Console for power users, or keep internal only? Proposal: surface just one slider (latency vs throughput) that maps to a preset of the knobs.
- Explore adaptive skim thresholds: use short-term EWMA of queue dispersion to auto-tune skim_age_threshold and occupancy gating.
- Measure interaction with routing fallbacks (e.g., when fallback to smaller models occurs) to ensure skims don't amplify model-change churn.
- Run on private deployment images (on-prem customers) to verify different NICs and kernel versions don't change regime.

Quick reproduction commands (local test harness):
- Start test harness: ./tools/benchmarks/run_mixed_workload --config configs/mixed_interactive_burst.json --duration 90 --seed 42 --out run01.json
- Toggle skim in local runtime: curl -XPOST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "http://localhost:9000/admin/coalescer/config" -d '{"skim_enabled": true, "skim_age_threshold_ms":25, "skim_max_size":6}'
- Collect metrics: ./tools/metrics/ingest_and_agg --input run01.json --out metrics01.csv

Appendix: quick heuristics checklist for engineers implementing the guardrail:
- Ensure skim path uses same execution thread pool as regular batches or a bounded separate pool to avoid starvation.
- When splitting KV cache ownership between skim and full batches, prefer shared read-only pointers to avoid copies.
- Emit a counter when skim causes a kernel selection change so we can triage odd throughput regressions quickly.

Notes to self: push a small RFC summarizing these results to infra-team and propose a limited alpha on two customer pools. Coordinate with SRE to add alerting for bulk throughput delta > 5% within 10m after enabling skims.

End of document.

next_steps: RFC -> alpha gate on 2 pools -> 6hr long-run stability -> iterate on adaptive thresholds
